chapters.title: הַמַּסָּע אֶל אוֹז הַגָּדוֹל
chapters.orig_title: The Journey to the Great Oz

s.line: They were obliged to camp out that night under a large tree in the forest, for there were no houses near.
s.note: נֶאֱלַץ (nif'al) = "was forced, had to". It is a little more formal than הָיָה צָרִיךְ and very common in the news: הַטַּיָּס נֶאֱלַץ לִנְחֹת (the pilot was forced to land). The active pi'el is אִלֵּץ = to force. בַּסְּבִיבָה = "in the area, nearby"; סְבִיבָה also means "environment".

s.line: The tree made a good, thick covering to protect them from the dew,
s.note: הֵגֵן עַל … מִפְּנֵי … = protected someone from something. Note the two prepositions: עַל the person, מִפְּנֵי the danger. The same root gives מָגֵן (shield), as in מָגֵן דָּוִד.

s.line: and the Tin Woodman chopped a great pile of wood with his axe
s.note: חָטַב = to chop wood; חוֹטֵב עֵצִים (a woodcutter) is its participle. עֵצִים is both "trees" and "wood, firewood".

s.line: and Dorothy built a splendid fire that warmed her and made her feel less lonely.
s.note: גָּרַם לְ… + infinitive = "made someone do/feel": הַסֶּרֶט גָּרַם לִי לִבְכּוֹת (the film made me cry). מְדוּרָה is an outdoor fire, a campfire; Israelis light them on Lag BaOmer. A fire in a fireplace or a building fire is אֵשׁ.

s.line: She and Toto ate the last of their bread,

w: מָה יִהְיֶה עִם|what would happen about|~idiom lit. what will be with
s.line: and now she did not know what they would do for breakfast.
s.note: מָה יִהְיֶה עִם …? = "what will become of …, what about …?", an everyday phrase: מָה יִהְיֶה עִם הַכֶּסֶף? Hebrew keeps the future יִהְיֶה after a past verb like לֹא יָדְעָה, where English shifts to "would".

s.line: “If you wish,” said the Lion, “I will go into the forest and kill a deer for you.
You can roast it by the fire, since your tastes are so peculiar that you prefer cooked food,
s.note: מְבֻשָּׁל (cooked) is a pu'al participle, the passive of pi'el בִּשֵּׁל (to cook). The same pair works for many kitchen words: טִגֵּן → מְטֻגָּן (fried). הֶעֱדִיף (hif'il) = to prefer; עֲדִיף = "it's better": עֲדִיף לְחַכּוֹת (better to wait).

w: תִּהְיֶה לָךְ|you will have|~lit. there will be to you (fem.)
s.line: and then you will have a very good breakfast.”
“Don’t! Please don’t,” begged the Tin Woodman.
s.note: הִתְחַנֵּן (hitpa'el) = to beg, plead; from the root of חֵן (grace, charm). אַל + future is the negative command: אַל תִּדְאַג (don't worry). Plain לֹא cannot be used this way.

w: הָיִיתִי בּוֹכֶה|I would cry|pa'al ptc · ב־כ־ה
s.line: “I should certainly weep if you killed a poor deer, and then my jaws would rust again.”
s.note: The unreal "if": <t>אִם הָיִיתָ הוֹרֵג …, הָיִיתִי בּוֹכֶה</t> = "if you killed …, I would cry". Both halves use <t>הָיָה</t> + present participle. You will hear it all the time: <t>אִם הָיָה לִי זְמַן, הָיִיתִי בָּא</t> (if I had time, I'd come). <t>הֶחְלִיד</t> (to rust) and <t>חָלוּד</t> (rusty) share the root ח־ל־ד.

s.line: But the Lion went away into the forest and found his own supper, and no one ever knew what it was, for he didn’t mention it.
s.note: הִזְכִּיר (hif'il of ז־כ־ר) = to mention, and also to remind: תַּזְכִּיר לִי מָחָר (remind me tomorrow). Its relatives: זָכַר (remembered), נִזְכַּר (recalled), תִּזְכֹּרֶת (a reminder, as on your phone).

s.line: And the Scarecrow found a tree full of nuts and filled Dorothy’s basket with them, so that she would not be hungry for a long time.
s.note: מָלֵא is the adjective "full"; מִלֵּא is the pi'el verb "to fill" (מִלֵּא טֹפֶס = filled in a form). כְּדֵי שֶׁ + future = "so that": the verb after it is always future, even in a past story.

s.line: She thought this was very kind and thoughtful of the Scarecrow,
s.note: מִתְחַשֵּׁב = considerate, thoughtful of others; the verb הִתְחַשֵּׁב בְּ… = to take someone into account. It comes from חָשַׁב (to think). מִצַּד = "on the part of": זֶה יָפֶה מִצִּדְּךָ (that's nice of you).

w: מִכָּל הַלֵּב|heartily|~idiom with all the heart
s.line: but she laughed heartily at the awkward way in which the poor creature picked up the nuts.
s.note: צָחַק עַל = to laugh at (also "to make fun of"); צָחַק מִ… = to laugh at a joke. שֶׁבָּהּ = "in which": שֶׁ + בָּהּ, pointing back to the feminine דֶּרֶךְ. Hebrew relative clauses work like this: הַבַּיִת שֶׁגַּרְתִּי בּוֹ (the house I lived in).

s.line: His padded hands were so clumsy and the nuts were so small that he dropped almost as many as he put in the basket.
s.note: הִפִּיל is the hif'il of נָפַל (fell): "to make fall", that is, to drop. Hif'il often adds "make/cause". מְגֻשָּׁם (clumsy) and מְסֻרְבָּל (awkward) look like pu'al participles but are just adjectives, with no passive meaning. אַתָּה מְגֻשָּׁם! is a common teasing remark.

w: לֹא הָיָה אִכְפַּת|did not mind|~idiom: לְX אִכְפַּת = X cares
לָקַח לוֹ|it took him|~lit. (it) took to him
s.line: But the Scarecrow did not mind how long it took him to fill the basket,
s.note: אִכְפַּת לִי = I care; לֹא אִכְפַּת לִי = I don't care, I don't mind. The person goes with לְ, so here it is לַדַּחְלִיל. A very common word: לְמִי אִכְפַּת? (who cares?).

s.line: for it enabled him to keep away from the fire,
as he feared a spark might get into his straw and burn him up.
s.note: A reminder: after פָּחַד שֶׁ the verb is future (יִכָּנֵס, יִשְׂרֹף). הִתְרַחֵק (hitpa'el) = to move away, from רָחוֹק (far); its opposite is הִתְקָרֵב (to come near), in the next sentence.

w: שָׁמַר עַל מֶרְחָק|kept a distance|~set phrase
s.line: So he kept a good distance away from the flames, and only came near to cover Dorothy with dry leaves when she lay down to sleep.
s.note: שָׁמַר עַל מֶרְחָק = kept his distance. You will know the noun from public signs: שְׁמִירַת מֶרְחָק (social distancing). שָׁמַר עַל = to keep, guard, take care of: תִּשְׁמֹר עַל עַצְמְךָ (take care of yourself).

w: הָיָה לָהּ חַם|she was warm|~lit. it was warm to her
s.line: These kept her very snug and warm, and she slept soundly until morning.
s.note: חַם לָהּ = "she is warm" (lit. "it is warm to her"). For how you feel, Hebrew uses this pattern: קַר לִי, נָעִים לִי. שֵׁנָה (sleep) and שָׁנָה (year) are both spelled שנה without niqqud.

s.line: When it was daylight, the girl bathed her face in a little rippling brook,
s.note: פָּנִים (face) is always plural in form, so "her face" is הַפָּנִים שֶׁלָּהּ and it takes plural adjectives: פָּנִים יָפוֹת. נַחַל is a stream or creek; in Israel it is also a dry riverbed (wadi) used for hiking trails.

w: יָצְאוּ לַדֶּרֶךְ|set out|~idiom went out to the road
s.line: and soon after they all started toward the Emerald City.
s.note: יָצָא לַדֶּרֶךְ = "set out, started a journey". It is also used of projects: הַפְּרוֹיֶקְט יוֹצֵא לַדֶּרֶךְ (the project is getting under way).

w: עָתִיד|going|~set phrase: עָתִיד לְ = destined to
s.line: This was to be an eventful day for the travelers.
s.note: עָתִיד לְ… = "was going to, was destined to", a common written phrase: הַבִּנְיָן עָתִיד לְהִפָּתַח בַּקַּיִץ (the building is due to open in the summer). As a noun, הֶעָתִיד = the future, and also the name of the future tense.

w: עַד כַּמָּה שֶׁהָעַיִן מַגִּיעָה|as far as the eye could see|~idiom as far as the eye reaches
s.line: They had hardly been walking an hour when they saw before them a great ditch that crossed the road and divided the forest as far as they could see on either side.
s.note: בְּקֹשִׁי … כְּשֶׁ… = "hardly … when". בְּקֹשִׁי alone = barely, with difficulty: בְּקֹשִׁי שָׁמַעְתִּי (I could barely hear). חָצָה = to cross; at a crosswalk you will see מַעֲבַר חֲצִיָּה. חֵצִי (half) is from the same root.

s.line: It was a very wide ditch,
and when they crept up to the edge and looked into it they could see it was also very deep,
s.note: הֵצִיץ (hif'il) = to peek, take a quick look: הֵצַצְתִּי בַּטֶּלֶפוֹן (I glanced at the phone). זָחַל = to crawl; a baby זוֹחֵל, and so does a זָחָל (caterpillar).

s.line: and there were many big, jagged rocks at the bottom.
The sides were so steep that none of them could climb down,
and for a moment it seemed that their journey must end.
s.note: נִדְמֶה לִי = "it seems to me, I think": נִדְמֶה לִי שֶׁרָאִיתִי אוֹתוֹ (I think I saw him). It is a little softer and more literary than נִרְאֶה לִי. הִסְתַּיֵּם (hitpa'el) = to come to an end; the end of something is סִיּוּם.

s.line: “What shall we do?” asked Dorothy despairingly.
s.note: בְּיֵאוּשׁ: Hebrew often makes an adverb from בְּ + a noun, where English adds "-ly": בְּשִׂמְחָה (gladly), בְּשֶׁקֶט (quietly). מִתְיָאֵשׁ (giving up hope) is from the same root, as in אַל תִּתְיָאֵשׁ! (don't give up!).

w: אֵין לִי|I have no|~lit. there is not to me
שֶׁמֶץ שֶׁל מֻשָּׂג|the faintest idea|~idiom a trace of a notion
s.line: “I haven’t the faintest idea,” said the Tin Woodman,
s.note: אֵין לִי שֶׁמֶץ שֶׁל מֻשָּׂג = "I haven't the faintest idea". The everyday short form is אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג (no idea).

w: שָׁקוּעַ בְּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת|lost in thought|~idiom sunk in thoughts
s.line: and the Lion shook his shaggy mane and looked thoughtful.
s.note: שָׁקוּעַ בְּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת = "lost in thought", lit. "sunk in thoughts". שָׁקַע = to sink; שְׁקִיעָה = sunset, when the sun "sinks". פָּרוּעַ = wild, messy (of hair); שֵׂעָר פָּרוּעַ = unkempt hair.

s.line: But the Scarecrow said, “We cannot fly, that is certain.
Neither can we climb down into this great ditch.
s.note: Hebrew can put the infinitive first for emphasis: <t>גַּם לָרֶדֶת … אֲנַחְנוּ לֹא יְכוֹלִים</t> = "climb down … we can't either". This fronting is common in speech: <t>לְבַשֵּׁל אֲנִי לֹא יוֹדֵעַ</t> (cooking, I don't know how).

s.line: Therefore, if we cannot jump over it, we must stop where we are.”
s.note: נִצְטָרֵךְ = "we will need to, we'll have to", hitpa'el of צָרִיךְ. In hitpa'el, when the root starts with צ, the ת swaps places with it and turns into ט: הִצְטָרֵךְ, not "hitzarekh". So also הִצְטַעֵר (to be sorry).

s.line: “I think I could jump over it,” said the Cowardly Lion, after measuring the distance carefully in his mind.
s.note: מָדַד = to measure; מִדָּה = size, as in a shop: אֵיזוֹ מִדָּה אַתָּה? (what size are you?). Hebrew puts calculations בָּרֹאשׁ "in the head": חִשַּׁבְתִּי בָּרֹאשׁ (I worked it out in my head).

w: הַכֹּל בְּסֵדֶר|we're all right|~idiom all is in order
אֶחָד אַחֲרֵי הַשֵּׁנִי|one at a time|~idiom one after the other
s.line: “Then we are all right,” answered the Scarecrow, “for you can carry us all over on your back, one at a time.”
s.note: הֶעֱבִיר (hif'il of עָבַר, to pass) = "to make pass": to carry across, transfer, hand over. הֶעֱבַרְתִּי לְךָ כֶּסֶף = I transferred you money; תַּעֲבִיר לִי אֶת הַמֶּלַח = pass me the salt.

s.line: “Well, I’ll try it,” said the Lion.
“Who will go first?”
“I will,” declared the Scarecrow, “for, if you found that you could not jump over the gulf, Dorothy would be killed, or the Tin Woodman badly dented on the rocks below.
s.note: תֵּהָרֵג = "will be killed", nif'al (passive) of הָרַג (to kill). The news uses this form: שְׁנַיִם נֶהֶרְגוּ בַּתְּאוּנָה (two were killed in the accident). מִתְבָּרֵר שֶׁ… = "it turns out that …", very common in speech. הִכְרִיז = to announce; הַכְרָזָה = an announcement.

w: מְשַׁנֶּה|matters|~idiom: זֶה לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה = it doesn't matter
s.line: But if I am on your back it will not matter so much, for the fall would not hurt me at all.”
s.note: זֶה לֹא מְשַׁנֶּה = "it doesn't matter", lit. "it doesn't change (anything)"; מְשַׁנֶּה is the pi'el participle of שִׁנָּה. הִזִּיק לְ… (hif'il) = to harm; נֵזֶק = damage, and on cigarette packs you see מַזִּיק (harmful).

w: שֶׁאֵין בְּרֵרָה|that there is no choice|~idiom
s.line: “I am terribly afraid of falling, myself,” said the Cowardly Lion, “but I suppose there is nothing to do but try it.
s.note: מְנִיחַ (hif'il of נ־ו־ח) = I suppose, assume; also "to put down, place". The noun הַנָּחָה means both "assumption" and "discount" in a shop. אֵין בְּרֵרָה אֶלָּא … = "there's no choice but …". אֵין בְּרֵרָה alone is one of the most-used phrases in Israel.

s.line: So get on my back and we will make the attempt.”
s.note: In speech, the future often serves as a polite command: <t>תַּעֲלֶה</t> rather than the formal imperative <t>עֲלֵה</t>. <t>נִסָּיוֹן</t> (attempt, experience) shares its root with <t>נִסָּה</t> (to try).

s.line: The Scarecrow sat upon the Lion’s back,
and the big beast walked to the edge of the gulf and crouched down.
s.note: חַיָּה (animal, beast) is feminine, so the verbs are feminine (הָלְכָה, הִשְׁתּוֹפְפָה) even though the Lion is male. Grammar follows the word, not the animal. הִשְׁתּוֹפֵף: as with צ, a root starting with שׁ swaps places with the ת of hitpa'el.

s.line: “Why don’t you run and jump?” asked the Scarecrow.
s.note: A run-up before a jump is <t>תְּנוּפָה</t>; you will hear <t>לָקַח תְּנוּפָה</t> = "took a run-up", and also "gathered momentum".

s.line: “Because that isn’t the way we Lions do these things,” he replied.
s.note: הֵשִׁיב (hif'il of שׁ־ו־ב, "to return") = to reply, a bookish synonym of עָנָה; תְּשׁוּבָה = an answer. It also means "to give back": הֵשִׁיב אֶת הַכֶּסֶף.

s.line: Then giving a great spring,
he shot through the air and landed safely on the other side.
s.note: טָס = to fly fast, or to fly by plane: מָחָר אֲנִי טָס לְחוּ"ל (tomorrow I fly abroad). נָחַת בְּשָׁלוֹם = landed safely, what you text after a flight. נְחִיתָה = landing.

s.line: They were all greatly pleased to see how easily he did it,
and after the Scarecrow had got down from his back the Lion sprang across the ditch again.
s.note: בַּחֲזָרָה = back (to where you came from), from חָזַר: תֵּן לִי אֶת זֶה בַּחֲזָרָה = give it back to me.

w: הַבָּאָה בַּתּוֹר|next|~idiom the next in line
s.line: Dorothy thought she would go next;
s.note: הַבָּא בַּתּוֹר = "next in line", from תּוֹר (a queue, also an appointment: קָבַעְתִּי תּוֹר לָרוֹפֵא, I made a doctor's appointment). מִי הַבָּא בַּתּוֹר? = who's next?

w: עַל הַיָּדַיִם|in her arms|~idiom lit. on the hands
s.line: so she took Toto in her arms and climbed on the Lion’s back, holding tightly to his mane with one hand.
s.note: כְּשֶׁהִיא מַחְזִיקָה = "(while) holding": כְּשֶׁ + pronoun + participle is how Hebrew says an English "-ing" clause. הֶחְזִיק בְּ… = to hold on to; חָזָק (strong) is from the same root. לָקַח עַל הַיָּדַיִם = to pick up (a child, a pet).

s.line: The next moment it seemed as if she were flying through the air;
s.note: עָפָה can be past ("she flew") or present ("she is flying"): in ע־ו verbs the feminine singular past and present are spelled the same and differ only in stress (past עָפָה on the first syllable, present on the last). Here כְּאִלּוּ shows it is present.

s.line: and then, before she had time to think about it, she was safe on the other side.
s.note: הִסְפִּיק (hif'il) = "to have time to, to manage in time", a very common verb: לֹא הִסְפַּקְתִּי לֶאֱכֹל (I didn't get a chance to eat). It also means "to be enough": זֶה מַסְפִּיק (that's enough).

s.line: The Lion went back a third time and got the Tin Woodman,
s.note: הֵבִיא is the hif'il of בָּא (came): "to make come" = to bring.

s.line: and then they all sat down for a few moments to give the beast a chance to rest,
s.note: הִזְדַּמְּנוּת = a chance, opportunity. It comes from זְמַן (time) via the hitpa'el הִזְדַּמֵּן (to happen to come along): אִם תִּזְדַּמֵּן לְתֵל אָבִיב (if you happen to be in Tel Aviv). Here too the ת of hitpa'el changes, to ד after ז.

s.line: for his great leaps had made his breath short,
s.note: קֹצֶר נְשִׁימָה = shortness of breath, also the medical term. Compare קֹצֶר רוּחַ = impatience (lit. shortness of spirit).

s.line: and he panted like a big dog that has been running too long.
They found the forest very thick on this side, and it looked dark and gloomy.
s.note: סָבוּךְ = tangled, dense (of a forest). The pu'al מְסֻבָּךְ, from the same root, is the everyday word for "complicated": זֶה מְסֻבָּךְ (it's complicated).

w: בְּדֶרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|on the yellow brick road
s.line: After the Lion had rested they started along the road of yellow brick,

w: בֵּינוֹ לְבֵין עַצְמוֹ|to himself|~idiom between him and himself
s.line: silently wondering, each in his own mind, if ever they would come to the end of the woods and reach the bright sunshine again.
s.note: בֵּינוֹ לְבֵין עַצְמוֹ = "to himself, privately", lit. "between him and himself"; for a woman בֵּינָהּ לְבֵין עַצְמָהּ. תָּהָה = to wonder; תְּהִיָּה = a question in one's mind. אֵי פַּעַם = ever: הָיִיתָ אֵי פַּעַם בְּאֵילַת? (have you ever been to Eilat?).

w: וּכְאִלּוּ זֶה לֹא מַסְפִּיק|as if that weren't enough|~idiom
s.line: To add to their discomfort, they soon heard strange noises in the depths of the forest,
s.note: וּכְאִלּוּ זֶה לֹא מַסְפִּיק = "and as if that weren't enough", a fixed phrase in speech and in the news. עַד מְהֵרָה = soon, before long; a bit literary. בִּמְהֵרָה is used the same way, and מַהֵר (quickly) has the same root.

s.line: and the Lion whispered to them that it was in this part of the country that the Kalidahs lived.
s.note: Reported speech keeps the present: <t>לָחַשׁ שֶׁ… גָּרוֹת</t> "whispered that … (they) live". The verb comes before the subject here, which Hebrew allows after a place phrase. The Kalidahs are <t>חַיּוֹת</t> (feminine), so: <t>גָּרוֹת</t>.

s.line: “What are the Kalidahs?” asked the girl.
s.note: מָה זֶה …? is how to ask "what is/are …?" about anything, singular or plural: מָה זֶה פֶלָאפֶל?. זֶה does not change here.

w: וְיֵשׁ לָהֶן|and they have|~lit. there is to them (fem.)
s.line: “They are monstrous beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers,” replied the Lion, “and with claws so long and sharp that they could tear me in two as easily as I could kill Toto.
s.note: צִפָּרְנַיִם = claws, and also your fingernails: לָק לְצִפָּרְנַיִם = nail polish. מִפְלֶצֶת = a monster; מִפְלַצְתִּי is its adjective (monstrous, also "huge" in slang). קָרַע = to tear; קֶרַע = a tear, a rift.

s.line: I’m terribly afraid of the Kalidahs.”
s.note: פָּחַד מִ…: to be afraid of takes מִ. נוֹרָא (terrible) works as an adverb in speech, "terribly, really": נוֹרָא יָפֶה (really pretty), נוֹרָא חַם הַיּוֹם.

s.line: “I’m not surprised that you are,” returned Dorothy.
s.note: מֻפְתָּע = surprised, a hof'al participle: the passive of hif'il הִפְתִּיעַ (to surprise). A surprise party is מְסִבַּת הַפְתָּעָה. Hif'il and hof'al pair like this: הִזְמִין invited → מֻזְמָן invited (guest).

s.line: “They must be dreadful beasts.”
s.note: בֶּטַח = "surely, probably, must be": הוּא בֶּטַח עָיֵף (he must be tired). Alone it means "sure!": – אַתָּה בָּא? – בֶּטַח!

w: עָמַד לַעֲנוֹת|was about to reply|~idiom עָמַד לְ = was about to
s.line: The Lion was about to reply when suddenly they came to another gulf across the road.
s.note: עָמַד לְ… + infinitive = "was about to": הָאוֹטוֹבּוּס עוֹמֵד לָצֵאת (the bus is about to leave). Literally "stood to …". נוֹסָף = additional, another; בְּנוֹסָף = in addition.

s.line: But this one was so broad and deep that the Lion knew at once he could not leap across it.
So they sat down to consider what they should do,
s.note: שָׁקַל = to weigh, and so "to consider": אֲנִי שׁוֹקֵל לַעֲבֹר דִּירָה (I'm thinking of moving). The coin שֶׁקֶל is from the same root; it was first a unit of weight.

s.line: and after serious thought the Scarecrow said:
“Here is a great tree, standing close to the ditch.
If the Tin Woodman can chop it down, so that it will fall to the other side, we can walk across it easily.”
s.note: אִם … יַצְלִיחַ: a real "if" about the future takes the future tense in Hebrew, where English uses the present "can". כָּרַת = to cut down (a tree); כְּרִיתַת יְעָרוֹת = deforestation.

s.line: “That is a first-rate idea,” said the Lion.
s.note: מְצֻיָּן (excellent) is in form a pu'al participle of צִיֵּן (to mark, to note), roughly "marked out". In school it is the top grade, and כְּפִי שֶׁצֻּיַּן = "as was noted" is common in the news.

w: שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְךָ|that you have|~lit. there is to you
s.line: “One would almost suspect you had brains in your head, instead of straw.”
s.note: חָשַׁד = to suspect; חָשַׁד בְּ… = to suspect someone, and the noun חָשׁוּד = a suspect, a news word: הַחָשׁוּד נֶעֱצַר (the suspect was arrested). אֶפְשָׁר + infinitive = "one can".

s.line: The Woodman set to work at once,
s.note: נִגַּשׁ לָעֲבוֹדָה = "got down to work". נִגַּשׁ = to approach, go up to; נִגַּשׁ לְמִבְחָן = to sit an exam. Compare נָגִישׁ = accessible (for wheelchairs).

s.line: and so sharp was his axe that the tree was soon chopped nearly through.
s.note: נֶחְתַּךְ = was cut, the nif'al passive of חָתַךְ (to cut). Active חָתַכְתִּי אֶת הַלֶּחֶם → passive הַלֶּחֶם נֶחְתַּךְ. Also: נֶחְתַּכְתִּי = I cut myself.

w: בְּכָל הַכֹּחַ|with all his might|~idiom with all the strength
s.line: Then the Lion put his strong front legs against the tree and pushed with all his might,
s.note: דָּחַף = to push. On Israeli doors you will see דְּחֹף (push) and מְשֹׁךְ (pull). הִצְמִיד = to press something against; צָמוּד = close, attached, as in a company car, רֶכֶב צָמוּד.

s.line: and slowly the big tree tipped and fell with a crash across the ditch, with its top branches on the other side.
s.note: נָטָה = to lean, tip; also "to tend to": הוּא נוֹטֶה לְהַסְכִּים (he tends to agree). The noun נְטִיָּה = a tendency. לְרֹחַב = across, along the width, from רָחָב (wide).

s.line: They had just started to cross this queer bridge when a sharp growl made them all look up,
s.note: הֵרִים (hif'il, root ר־ו־ם) = to raise, lift: הֵרִים טֵלֵפוֹן = he phoned (lit. lifted a phone), הֵרִים אֶת הָרֹאשׁ = looked up. רָם = high, loud: בְּקוֹל רָם (out loud).

w: וּלְמַרְבֵּה הַזְּוָעָה|and to their horror|~set phrase to the great horror
s.line: and to their horror they saw running toward them two great beasts with bodies like bears and heads like tigers.
s.note: לְמַרְבֵּה … + noun = "to (one's) great …": לְמַרְבֵּה הַמַּזָּל (luckily), לְמַרְבֵּה הַצַּעַר (unfortunately), לְמַרְבֵּה הַהַפְתָּעָה (surprisingly). לִקְרַאת = toward; also "ahead of, in preparation for": לִקְרַאת הַחַג (ahead of the holiday).

s.line: “They are the Kalidahs!” said the Cowardly Lion, beginning to tremble.
s.note: רָעַד = to tremble, shake; רְעִידַת אֲדָמָה = an earthquake (lit. a trembling of the ground).

s.line: “Quick!” cried the Scarecrow.
“Let us cross over.”
s.note: בּוֹאוּ + future (we-form) = "let's": בּוֹאוּ נֵלֵךְ (let's go). To one person: בּוֹא נֵלֵךְ, בּוֹאִי נֵלֵךְ. מַהֵר is used both as "quickly" and as the command "hurry!".

w: עַל הַיָּדַיִם|in her arms|~idiom lit. on the hands
s.line: So Dorothy went first, holding Toto in her arms,
s.note: רִאשׁוֹנָה agrees with Dorothy: "she crossed first (fem.)". With the Scarecrow it was רִאשׁוֹן. Hebrew makes such words agree, while English "first" does not change.

s.line: the Tin Woodman followed, and the Scarecrow came next.
The Lion, although he was certainly afraid, turned to face the Kalidahs,
s.note: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = although, the standard written form; in speech you will also hear לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ and אַף שֶׁ. הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to turn around, and also "to wander around": הִסְתּוֹבַבְנוּ בָּעִיר (we walked around town).

s.line: and then he gave so loud and terrible a roar that Dorothy screamed and the Scarecrow fell over backward,
while even the fierce beasts stopped short and looked at him in surprise.
s.note: נֶעֱצַר (nif'al) usually means "stopped, came to a stop", active in meaning. But in the news it is often passive: הַחָשׁוּד נֶעֱצַר = the suspect was arrested (עָצַר = to stop, to arrest). הִבִּיט בְּ… = to look at, with בְּ.

s.line: But, seeing they were bigger than the Lion,
s.note: Comparison: <t>גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר מִ…</t> = bigger than. <t>יוֹתֵר</t> can also come first (<t>יוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל</t>), which is common in speech; <t>מִ</t> means "than".

s.line: and remembering that there were two of them and only one of him,
s.note: נִזְכַּר (nif'al) = "remembered, it came back to me": פִּתְאֹם נִזְכַּרְתִּי (suddenly I remembered). שְׁתַּיִם is feminine "two" for the Kalidahs; the Lion is אֶחָד, masculine.

s.line: the Kalidahs again rushed forward,
and the Lion crossed over the tree and turned to see what they would do next.
s.note: זִנֵּק (pi'el) = to leap, dash, rush forward; also used of prices: הַמְּחִירִים זִנְּקוּ (prices jumped). The starting gun in a race is זִנּוּק.

w: אַף לֹא לְרֶגַע|even for a moment|~set phrase
s.line: Without stopping an instant the fierce beasts also began to cross the tree.
s.note: הִתְעַכֵּב (hitpa'el) = to be delayed, to linger: הָרַכֶּבֶת מִתְעַכֶּבֶת (the train is delayed). עִכּוּב = a delay, an announcement you will hear at the airport.

s.line: And the Lion said to Dorothy:

w: הָלַךְ עָלֵינוּ|we are done for|~idiom lit. it went on us
s.line: “We are lost, for they will surely tear us to pieces with their sharp claws.
s.note: הָלַךְ עָלֵינוּ = "we're done for, it's all over for us". Very colloquial: הָלַךְ עָלַי (I'm finished). לִגְזָרִים = to shreds, to pieces; גֶּזֶר (carrot) is a different word.

s.line: But stand close behind me, and I will fight them as long as I am alive.”
s.note: נִלְחַם בְּ… = to fight (against) someone. It is nif'al but active in meaning; מִלְחָמָה (war) is from the same root. כָּל עוֹד = as long as: כָּל עוֹד יֵשׁ זְמַן.

s.line: “Wait a minute!” called the Scarecrow.
s.note: רֶגַע! = "wait!, hold on!" This one word is how Israelis interrupt or stop someone. רֶגַע אֶחָד or שְׁנִיָּה (a second) are the same.

s.line: He had been thinking what was best to be done,
and now he asked the Woodman to chop away the end of the tree that rested on their side of the ditch.
s.note: בִּקֵּשׁ מִ… = to ask (request) from someone: בִּקַּשְׁתִּי מִמֶּנּוּ עֶזְרָה. To ask a question is שָׁאַל. מֻנָּח = "placed, lying", the hof'al of הִנִּיחַ (to put down). The same word also means "a term": מֻנָּח מִקְצוֹעִי (a technical term).

s.line: The Tin Woodman began to use his axe at once,
s.note: הִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בְּ… = to use; the thing used takes בְּ: אֲנִי מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בַּמַּחְשֵׁב. Another שׁ root with the hitpa'el swap.

s.line: and, just as the two Kalidahs were nearly across, the tree fell with a crash into the gulf,
carrying the ugly, snarling brutes with it,
s.note: סָחַף = to sweep away (as a flood does); figuratively "to carry away": הַהוֹפָעָה סָחֲפָה אֶת הַקָּהָל (the show swept the audience away). סַחֲפָן = a charismatic speaker.

s.line: and both were dashed to pieces on the sharp rocks at the bottom.
s.note: הִתְרַסֵּק (hitpa'el) = to crash, be smashed to pieces; it is the news verb for a plane crash: מָטוֹס הִתְרַסֵּק. רִסֵּק (pi'el) = to smash, also to mash food: תַּפּוּחַ מְרֻסָּק (apple sauce).

s.line: “Well,” said the Cowardly Lion, drawing a long breath of relief, “I see we are going to live a little while longer, and I am glad of it,
s.note: הֲקָלָה = relief, from קַל (light, easy). The idiom for "breathed a sigh of relief" is נָשַׁם לִרְוָחָה. נוּ = "well, so": נוּ, מָה קָרָה? (so, what happened?). Said impatiently it means "come on!".

s.line: for it must be a very uncomfortable thing not to be alive.
s.note: בַּחַיִּים = alive, lit. "in life": הוּא כְּבָר לֹא בַּחַיִּים (he is no longer alive). It also means "ever": בַּחַיִּים לֹא! (never!). לֹא נוֹחַ = uncomfortable, awkward: לֹא נוֹחַ לִי לְבַקֵּשׁ (I feel awkward asking).

s.line: Those creatures frightened me so badly that my heart is beating yet.”
s.note: הִפְחִיד (hif'il) = to frighten, "to make afraid", from פָּחַד (feared). דָּפַק = to beat, knock: דָּפַק בַּדֶּלֶת (knocked on the door); דֹּפֶק = pulse.

w: שֶׁהָיָה לִי|that I had|~lit. there was to me
s.line: “Ah,” said the Tin Woodman sadly, “I wish I had a heart to beat.”
s.note: הַלְוַאי = "if only, I wish". For a wish about the future it takes the future: הַלְוַאי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מָחָר יוֹם יָפֶה; for something unreal now, the past: הַלְוַאי שֶׁהָיָה לִי (I wish I had).

s.line: This adventure made the travelers more anxious than ever to get out of the forest,
s.note: יוֹתֵר מִתָּמִיד = "more than ever" (lit. "more than always"): הַמְּחִירִים גְּבוֹהִים יוֹתֵר מִתָּמִיד. מְטַיֵּל = a traveler or hiker; טִיּוּל = a trip, a hike, or just a walk.

s.line: and they walked so fast that Dorothy became tired, and had to ride on the Lion’s back.
s.note: הִתְעַיֵּף (hitpa'el) = to get tired, from עָיֵף (tired). Hitpa'el often means "to become": הִתְרַגֵּשׁ (got excited), הִתְבַּגֵּר (grew up). רָכַב עַל = to ride (a horse, a bike); רֶכֶב = a vehicle.

s.line: To their great joy the trees became thinner the farther they advanced,
s.note: כְּכָל שֶׁ… , … יוֹתֵר = "the more …, the more …": כְּכָל שֶׁאַתָּה מִתְאַמֵּן יוֹתֵר, קַל יוֹתֵר (the more you practice, the easier it gets). נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) = "became": נַעֲשָׂה קַר (it got cold). It can also mean "was done".

s.line: and in the afternoon they suddenly came upon a broad river, flowing swiftly just before them.
s.note: אַחַר הַצָּהֳרַיִם = afternoon, often shortened in writing to אחה"צ. In speech many say אַחֲרֵי הַצָּהֳרַיִם. צָהֳרַיִם = noon, midday. זָרַם = to flow; זֶרֶם = current, also electric current.

w: דֶּרֶךְ הַלְּבֵנִים הַצְּהֻבּוֹת|the yellow brick road
s.line: On the other side of the water they could see the road of yellow brick running through a beautiful country,

w: הָיוּ בָּהּ|it had|~lit. there were in it
s.line: with green meadows dotted with bright flowers and all the road bordered with trees hanging full of delicious fruits.
s.note: מְנֻקָּד = dotted, a pu'al participle of נִקֵּד (to dot). It is also the word for text with vowel points: טֶקְסְט מְנֻקָּד, like this one. נִקּוּד (niqqud) and נְקֻדָּה (a dot, a point) share the root. עָמוּס = loaded, and so "busy, packed": יוֹם עָמוּס (a busy day).

s.line: They were greatly pleased to see this delightful country before them.
“How shall we cross the river?” asked Dorothy.
“That is easily done,” replied the Scarecrow.
“The Tin Woodman must build us a raft, so we can float to the other side.”
s.note: שָׁט = to sail, float on water; שַׁיִט = sailing, and אֳנִיַּת שַׁיִט is a cruise ship. צָרִיךְ + infinitive = must, needs to; it agrees with the subject: הִיא צְרִיכָה, הֵם צְרִיכִים.

s.line: So the Woodman took his axe and began to chop down small trees to make a raft,
and while he was busy at this the Scarecrow found on the riverbank a tree full of fine fruit.
s.note: עָסוּק = busy; עָסַק בְּ… = to be engaged in, deal with: בַּמֶּה אַתָּה עוֹסֵק? (what do you do for a living?). עֵסֶק = a business. גָּדָה = a riverbank; in the news הַגָּדָה הַמַּעֲרָבִית = the West Bank.

s.line: This pleased Dorothy, who had eaten nothing but nuts all day,
s.note: שִׂמֵּחַ (pi'el) = to make happy, gladden; שָׂמַח (pa'al) = to be glad, as in הֵם שָׂמְחוּ above. Pi'el often makes a pa'al verb causative like this.

w: אֲרוּחָה דְּשֵׁנָה|a hearty meal|~set phrase lit. a fat meal
s.line: and she made a hearty meal of the ripe fruit.
s.note: בָּשֵׁל = ripe, and מְבֻשָּׁל = cooked come from the same root ב־שׁ־ל: fruit is "cooked" by the sun. בָּשֵׁל also means "mature, ready": הַזְּמַן בָּשֵׁל (the time is ripe).

s.line: But it takes time to make a raft, even when one is as industrious and untiring as the Tin Woodman,
s.note: כְּשֶׁאַתָּה: Hebrew uses "you" for "one" (anyone), as English does in speech. בִּלְתִּי נִלְאֶה = "untiring, tireless", a fixed literary phrase: מַאֲמָץ בִּלְתִּי נִלְאֶה (a tireless effort). בִּלְתִּי = "un-, in-": בִּלְתִּי אֶפְשָׁרִי (impossible).

s.line: and when night came the work was not done.
s.note: יָרַד הַלַּיְלָה = night fell, lit. "went down". So also יָרַד גֶּשֶׁם (it rained) and יָרַד שֶׁלֶג (it snowed).

s.line: So they found a cozy place under the trees where they slept well until the morning;
and Dorothy dreamed of the Emerald City, and of the good Wizard Oz, who would soon send her back to her own home again.
s.note: הֶחֱזִיר (hif'il) = to return something, send back; חָזַר (pa'al) = to come back. הֶחֱזַרְתִּי אֶת הַסֵּפֶר = I returned the book. הַבַּיְתָה = homeward, "to home": the ending ָה means "toward", as in צָפוֹנָה (northward).
